Without some account of how God's knowledge relates to different possible things, His essence would either become identical with them or be made of parts. One possible account is that God's knowledge relates to existents as a definition relates to what it defines: an effect is an incomplete expression of its cause, while the cause expresses its effect in a higher way. — س قده

This view avoids saying that one simple being knows many different things in detail by saying it knows only the First Intellect in detail. But God's essence would still know two different things in detail: itself and the First Intellect. This brings back the earlier problem. — س قده

“At the level of His essence” means that the knowledge follows necessarily from God's essence; it does not mean that it is identical with the essence. The view differs from the theory of forms in God's essence because it combines general and detailed knowledge and gives each level of causes and effects its own degree of detail.
This is the earlier objection to forms present in God's essence: knowledge before creation cannot be something added to the essence.

The phrase may refer to another account of knowledge. Since the author did not list it among the recognized views, the note suggests that he may instead mean the theologians' account, in which divine attributes are considered in a causal order. — س قده
“Some earlier philosophers” may refer to Thales of Miletus. The author may instead have al-Tusi in mind, whom he elsewhere identifies with this view.
In the realized account, the First Intellect exists through God's existence and is eternal through God's eternity. In that sense, it might serve as God's knowledge. — س قده

The reasoning is: knowledge itself is necessary existence, and no essence is necessary existence. So no essence can itself be the reality of knowledge. The First Intellect has an essence; therefore it cannot be God's knowledge.

In mystical usage, “substance” means what is followed and depended on; “accident” means what depends on something else. The world's forms are dependent on the divine reality, so they are “accidents” in this sense, while God is the source they depend on. — س قده
Presence may be an essential feature of the thing that is present, but it is an active relation for the cause. An effect depends on its cause in its existence and detail. — ط مد ظله

The objection assumes that presence comes after the thing present. The reply is that presence may be drawn from the thing's existence and so be active knowledge in the realm of effects, not a later state in God.

A simple reality contains all things, and stronger existence means greater light and disclosure. The many names and forms differ in meaning, not as separate existences. A cause knows its effects more fully than they know themselves. — س قده

Knowledge is the condition in which something is present and makes other things present. It therefore belongs to light: light is its center and its true meaning. In God, the reality of light is complete. Indeed, God is the Light of Lights. All other lights—those that rule, those joined to souls, and those found in the material world—owe their light to Him. That is what calling Him the Light of Lights means.

A being whose own reality is true light without limit must be present to Himself through that very reality. By shining upon what is other than Himself, He also makes all other things present to Himself. How could anything in the unseen or the visible world be hidden from Him? Why would He need separate pictures or forms to make their objects known?
This is a strong argument if “light” means existence itself: the reality through which things are, which appears by itself and makes the natures of things apparent.

The forms we imagine can become as vivid as external things, or more vivid, while remaining our own knowledge. On this account, the world and everything we see are manifestations of the soul's light and are known through its relation to them. — س قده

“Illumination” points to two linked ideas: light makes things visible, and a cause has power over what proceeds from it. A cause therefore knows its effects through its direct relation to them, without needing their images to enter it. — س قده
God does not see through an organ, as human beings do. His whole existence is sight, hearing, and every other perfect way of perceiving.

The author rejects two kinds of image-based knowledge and one kind of direct self-perception. The only valid account is that the soul itself knows its bodily powers through its relation to them. A power cannot know itself through an inner image: that would either duplicate the image in one place or lead to an endless chain.

The point is not that sight proves all knowledge is a relation. The author first argues that sight works through an illuminating relation, then says God's knowledge can also work this way because His knowledge is described as sight.
The imagined form is drawn from the storehouse of images already formed in the mind.

The author has said that al-Tusi's view is nearly the same as Suhrawardī's. Suhrawardī applies illumination to bodies and bodily powers; al-Tusi says that God knows things through forms present in higher intellects and souls. The note explains how al-Tusi's account can be read consistently with that of Suhrawardī. — س قده

Every being free from matter is capable of understanding and can itself be understood. There is no barrier between such beings. Each therefore knows the others, whether they are above it, below it, or at the same level.

This explains the statement that intellectual beings receive forms of things that are not their own effects. The point is not that God knows some things directly and others by receiving images of them. God knows both these beings and the forms within them through their presence to Him. Nor does it mean that an intellect knows its own effects merely through representations. The intended distinction concerns things that are not its effects.

Such things include higher intellects that cause a lower intellect to exist, and intellects at the same level, neither of which causes the other. They also include, for each governing intellect, the material forms governed by other intellects. Each material form depends on the higher being responsible for it, not on the being responsible for a different form.

Why does an intellect know these other beings? Nothing separate from matter is hidden from another such being. Moreover, every intellect knows the Necessary Being, and everything else is His effect. Knowledge of a cause entails knowledge of its effects. All created things must therefore be knowable to every separate intellect, whether they are above it or below it. What lies below it as its own effect is known directly through presence.

Why are forms needed for things it does not cause? When the thing known is neither identical with the knower nor subject to it as an effect, its form must be brought before the knower. Thus an intellect knows higher intellects and those alongside it through forms, since it does not govern them.

God, however, knows everything directly. Every being is either His immediate effect or the effect of one of His effects. The condition for direct knowledge of another—the complete power by which it is made present—is fulfilled in His case for all beings. He knows Himself as the cause of the first effect and thereby knows that effect. The first effect causes the second, which is also known directly through its cause, and the same applies throughout the order of existence. Similarly, each separate intellect directly knows what lies beneath it as its own effect, through its power to illuminate and govern it. The higher principles therefore know directly even the bodies that depend on them, all the more so the First Principle of all principles.
Because the First Cause has power over everything, it knows material things directly through the same light by which it brings them into being. — س قده

The separate intellects and souls know some things through their own forms; God knows those beings and their forms directly, without another form representing them. The account therefore aims to cover both universal and particular things. — س قده
This view does not actually refute God's prior care. It only fails to prove it. Those who rely on the view must offer another account of divine knowledge and care.

The objection is that “illumination” may be only a name for an ordinary relation. If existence itself is treated as only an idea, and essences are dark in themselves, then the relation cannot explain how things become known. — س قده
A thought can match or fail to match reality. This difference belongs to image-based knowledge, not to direct knowledge of a thing present to the knower. — ط مد ظله

The author allows that direct knowledge is not divided into concepts and judgments. His objection is that the illuminationist account makes all knowledge a relation, while knowledge is one light and perfection, not an empty relation.
The same objection applies to the previous point: perception has recognized forms, and this account must show where illumination fits among them. — ط مد ظله

Suppose the objection means that God, or any immaterial being, directly perceives particular material things, and calls that perception “sensation.” We can accept the implication and deny that it is absurd. Those who say that God's knowledge is a kind of sight do not shrink from this conclusion. Thinkers who say that God hears and sees but needs no bodily organs—including the author—must mean that every existent is directly present to Him. Visible, audible, and other particular things are among those existents. He therefore sees and hears them directly, not merely by knowing general descriptions of them.

For us, particular things become present through bodily senses because we need them. For God, they are present through His own essence. As the reports put it, His whole being is hearing and His whole being is sight.

But if the objection uses “sensation” to mean a bodily faculty housed in an organ, the implication fails. Direct perception of particulars is not the same as possessing a material sense-organ. “Perception” can sometimes be contrasted with abstract understanding or knowledge. The difficult case here is the material particular, which has position, extension, and quantity. An immaterial particular presents no comparable problem: understanding a separate intellect or an immaterial particular is an act of intellect. That is why it is said that every immaterial being knows itself.

The classification concerns what is known in itself. A body may be known through its image without being known as a body in itself, just as a visible thing is known through light or color rather than as an object of sight in every respect. — س قده
This refers to the author's view that perceptible forms are living, immaterial forms in the world of intellect. — س قده

The claim that each changing material thing has an enduring, intellectual form is one way to support the existence of Plato's separate Forms. If material beings were already directly known, the separate forms would not be needed. — س قده
A relation that is simply a category of thought may come after its two terms. An illuminating relation, which is grounded in existence, need not be later in that way. — ط مد ظله

The author says elsewhere that material bodies cannot be known in themselves because their parts and motions are hidden from one another. The note points out that this objection may be answered by treating their movement as one continuous whole. — ط مد ظله
This claim seems to conflict with the author's earlier suggestion that al-Tusi has a different view. The note says that his account may be closer to Suhrawardī's than it first appears. — س قده
The same problem applies to sight: the soul does not control external objects, so illumination alone cannot explain how it sees them.
The author distinguishes between God's active knowledge in creating things, which is true on this view, and His complete knowledge before creation, which it does not explain. — ط مد ظله

The author does not reject every kind of general knowledge of things. A simple being knows itself in detail and thereby knows all else in a general, unified way. What he rejects is an incomplete account that knows things only through their effects after they appear. — س قده

Two questions arise. First, the author elsewhere says that divine forms are separate intellects, but here says that the divine knowledge is the existence of things in God. He may be using “forms” in another sense or pointing to how closely each thing's intellectual existence is joined to its divine existence. Second, “reality” may mean the thing itself or the world of intellect. In either case, divine existence is the thing in its fullest and highest form.

In other words, this knowledge is independent as existence and light, but follows the known things in the ways their particular meanings appear within it. It is not created by them; it reveals what is implicit in the divine names and fixed realities. — س قده
“Keys” can mean the keys to a treasury or the treasuries themselves. The second meaning is supported by other verses, which speak of God's treasuries but not of keys to them.
These forms are not known by themselves, because they are absorbed in witnessing God. They are known only as His lights, and only God fully knows them. — س قده

This account treats God's oneness as the highest level of existence, without limit. Other levels are real but lower. In other philosophical and mystical accounts, only God's existence is fully real and all other existence is secondary. The names and attributes belong to a level below the essence, even though they are not things added to it.

If the broader kind were literally a part of the defining feature, the defining feature would also be a species, and the broader kind would have to belong to it in the same way. The author rejects this: the broader kind meaning is present in the form's existence, but is not a separate part of it. — س قده

At first sight, it is difficult to say that a distinguishing feature or a form is itself a kind of existence. Existence has no broader kind, no defining feature, and nothing corresponding to them. Also, saying that something is a kind of existence does not, by itself, mean it lacks an essence. Whiteness, for example, is a kind of being, but we can still say what whiteness is.

Consider the real features from which definitions are drawn. A body's bodily form corresponds to its capacity to have three dimensions. The plant soul corresponds to growing. The sensing and moving soul corresponds to sensation and movement by choice. Surely each of these has a nature we can describe. Otherwise nothing would have an essence at all.

The answer is that the author is speaking particularly about the defining perfections of substances such as rational souls and separate intellects. Following the Illuminationist philosopher, he often says that human souls and intellects are pure lights, or pure existences, without a separate limited essence. An essence, in this account, is a concept that describes an existence confined within limits. Intellects are not confined in that way; souls, too, do not remain fixed within a single limit.

A little later he will deny that the kinds of animal life below humanity possess distinct, positive defining perfections of this sort. The differences used in their definitions are ways in which their more general nature grows stronger. These differences are not separate existences added to the animal, but they are not mere absences either: an absence could not help make something the kind of thing it is. The final positive perfection, on this account, is the human being's holy or rational soul, a way of existing rather than an additional essence.
The many meanings do not weaken simplicity. They show that one existence gathers more perfections, loses less, and shines more fully. — س قده

Otherwise the human being could not be the last and most complete kind, gathering the earlier kinds within it. Or it would have to be put together from features that stand alongside one another rather than forming an ordered whole. There is a distinction here between considering the human being and a horse as separate kinds, and considering how lower forms are gathered into higher ones. When we consider the earlier forms as distinct things, they are like matter in relation to the last form. When we consider what they share without separating them from what completes them, they are wider kinds, and the final distinguishing feature gives them their completed identity.

This is one meaning of the saying, ‘The greater world is folded within you.’ Someone might object: how could a wider kind exist without its distinguishing feature, or matter without form, when the feature or form is what makes it complete? The reply is that denying a particular feature does not deny the more general reality. In the final kind, its last distinguishing feature completes all the wider kinds, and its last form completes all earlier material levels. This fits especially well with the view that the soul changes in its very existence until it becomes united with the active intellect. That intellect, by God's permission, brings natural kinds to their completion and gathers what is actual in them, just as prime matter gathers their possibilities.
A simpler way of stating the point is that animal life may count as a complete kind among animals but, in the human being, is included within a fuller reality.

God is the source who gives existence to all beings directly, and through their existence gives rise to all the different kinds of things. One principle therefore requires that every form of existence be present in Him in a higher, simpler, and more complete way. Other principles require that He be the source of every meaning and concept, without those meanings existing within Him as separate, limited things.

His knowledge of His own complete existence is thus the very same as His knowledge of all existences and all kinds. Because His existence is one and simple, that knowledge is also one. Yet it reveals all things distinctly. Existence is light, and the stronger that light becomes, the more clearly things can be disclosed. If different meanings are distinguishable through the weak, scattered lights of the world, they can be disclosed still more clearly in the single, powerful light of the eternal source. Their unity there does not erase their differences.

That explanation follows the author's own principles. The explanation favored by some mystics instead says that God pours out the kinds of things through His names and the forms of those names. In that account their fixed realities are present in the divine names. As they put it, glory belongs to the One who joins unity to unity and multiplicity to multiplicity. That approach will be discussed later.
An objection: this may explain God's direct and complete knowledge of things eternally, before they appear. But how can He already know them as actual effects, since they come into existence in time?

The answer is that the existence spread through things is the appearance of one reality in many forms. The earlier account described many things contained in one source; this describes one source appearing through many things. These two levels are not separate realities. Created existence depends on its source like a word whose meaning depends on its connection to other words. It cannot stand alone, and whatever is true of it is grounded in that source. Seen as a whole, the existence spread through many things is still one light, while also disclosing each thing in detail. It belongs to the divine order and is prior to created things by the priority of its source, not by being an earlier event in time.

Furthermore, the kinds present in divine knowledge are the very kinds that appear in the world. Their existence in knowledge is complete in a way that embraces the limited forms they later have. To grasp the complete reality is to grasp what appears from it. Once we understand how cause and effect belong together, the difficulty falls away.

The question of divine knowledge is central to theology. Many other questions can be understood through it, especially the unity of God. The claim that the one, simple reality includes all beings in a higher way is, at heart, a claim about direct divine knowledge. — س قده

This repeats the principle that a truly simple reality is all things in a higher way. Since God is fully present to Himself and nothing is absent from His unity, His self-knowledge is knowledge of all things.
A concept represents an essence when it describes a limited kind of existence. Concepts of God's names and attributes, by contrast, point to unlimited existence.
If God's existence does not belong to these meanings as their particular existence, then they are not essences belonging to God. They are meanings that appear through His existence.
“Potential” here can mean strength or power, not a readiness to exist. The unified divine existence is the power and source through which all separate existences appear.

When the forms are separate intellects, three questions arise. First, why do these intellects exist at all? That is not the issue here. The answer is that their existence is an expression of God's generosity. As His acts, they come from Him and return to Him as their beginning and end.

Second, why would God's knowledge of things need these intellects to carry the forms of other things, like books containing His knowledge? That question, too, is not the present one. The answer belongs to the account of the levels of knowledge. Because these intellects are actually immaterial, their knowledge is their very existence, even if it is not identical with what they are. An immaterial being knows itself and the things that come from it. The knowledge of one such being does not make the knowledge of another unnecessary. Each also counts as God's knowledge at the level of His acts, because its reality and what it knows are present to Him.

The third question is the one intended here. If God's own essence is already simple knowledge of all things, and if that one knowledge is detailed as well as simple, what need is there for forms alongside Him or for separate Platonic forms and lights? The author has already said that those who place God's detailed knowledge after His essence have not understood the point. Why, then, must these additional forms themselves be detailed knowledge? The following argument is meant to answer this third question. — س قده

The word here is a verbal noun linked to its object. An objection may be raised: knowing a cause must involve knowing its effects, but why must that knowledge take the form of separate images? If knowledge of the effects is already contained in knowledge of the cause itself, the principle is satisfied even more fully. So the question remains.

The reply lies in the author's words, “in the way in which it is its effect.” Knowing the cause means knowing each effect in its higher mode of existence, where it is present in its divine source. But it also means knowing that effect in its own mode of existence, as the actual effect that follows from the cause. On the account being discussed, this second kind of knowledge is through forms.

There is another objection. If these forms exist together with the knower, we can see how knowledge is through forms. But what if they exist separately as intelligences made of light? On the Platonic account, they are themselves acts of knowing. The reply is that, although they are knowledge in themselves, they are also independent forms through which material things are known. Seen in relation to God, they are His lights and His knowledge: they exist through Him and are eternal through His eternity. Seen as His effects in their own right, they are things known. The same realities can therefore be forms of knowledge in one respect and objects of knowledge in another. — س قده

Simple knowledge follows from the principle that a truly simple reality contains all existences. Detailed knowledge of things as effects follows from knowing their cause. This lets the author explain how the different accounts of divine knowledge fit together.

This passage explains more than the immediate question. It helps us understand the realm in which things were first known, divine decree and destiny, and the descent of spirits without their leaving their own higher level or changing their essential nature. It also explains how they can ascend without the higher level having changed.

The essence of a thing remains recognisable through its different appearances, and its ways of existing have one continuing source. So when a natural being descends to the lower level that belongs to its kind of existence, that descent can be described as the descent of its higher, divine or intellectual reality. Yet the higher reality has not abandoned its own level. When the natural being rises, its rising is truly a return to its higher source, because it has never been cut off from that source. The higher reality and the lower reflection are one truth understood at different levels.

The difficulty and the value of this knowledge lie in holding both sides together. Earth and matter have no place in the world beyond matter, yet what appears here is connected to that higher world and can rise toward the heavens and angels. Conversely, the world of bodies cannot contain a soul in its full reality, still less an intellect. Such beings have no bodily position or direction, yet their influence comes from their own source into this world, fills it, and gives it order. The Qur'an speaks of God ordering the affair from heaven to earth, “then it rises to Him.” The movement is real in the lower being, without requiring the higher source to change places. — س قده

Things do not literally break away from God as moisture separates from the sea. They are related to Him through their existence. God's essential existence is a stillness in the sense that nothing is waiting to happen and nothing changes in Him. — س قده
“The power of the moment” means that each reality receives existence according to its own capacity.

The passage about reaching the heavenly bodies might seem to say that individual souls, after passing through the levels of earthly bodies, attach themselves to one celestial sphere after another and finally unite with the universal Soul and universal Intellect. Some thinkers have understood the journey that way. But taken literally it would involve a soul passing from body to body, which is reincarnation. We should instead read the journey as a continuous rise in being: the soul develops and changes inwardly, through changes in its very existence.

On one interpretation, the “heavenly body” is the subtle spirit associated with the brain. Because it is refined and balanced, it resembles a celestial sphere; it carries the soul's powers, serves as the camp of its forces, and receives life. Or the phrase may refer to the enduring body of the world of images.

A better interpretation, in my view, is that the soul is attached to a heavenly body as something can appear through a visible form without becoming that form's soul. Suppose a person has an intense attachment to a beloved image and can encounter it only through a reflection in water or crystal. That does not make the person the soul of the water or crystal. Nor does the soul's reaching the universal Soul and universal Intellect mean it must literally inhabit each heavenly body in turn.

Skipping all those heavenly levels would look like a sudden leap, unless the soul had already advanced so far during earthly life that it no longer needed a body at all. The prophets may travel in that way, and there may be others. But someone still attached to the forms, pleasures, and habits of this world cannot pass beyond them without loosening those bonds completely. Such a person must turn away from constant concern with eating, drinking, and the other habits of bodily life, and cease clinging to sights, sounds, and passing particulars. — س قده
This rejects the claim that an effect needs its cause only to begin existing, but not to continue. The outpouring of existence does not stop.

In this usage, pure existence without any determination is the divine essence. When that same existence is considered through a perfection, it is a name: as self-manifesting and revealing all things, “Light”; as giving existence knowingly, “Powerful”; as revealing Himself and all things to Himself, “Knowing”; and as expressing the fixed realities, “Speaking.”
In the usual language of theologians, an attribute is a quality that exists in something else. — س قده
Theologians also use “essential attribute” for a feature without which a thing would not be what it is, or for a feature that makes similar things alike and different things distinct. — س قده

In mystical language, the attribute is the divine reality considered under a particular determination. The name is that reality together with the determination; the essence is the reality without that determination. These are not separate existences, so the names and attributes are not later additions to God.

“The essence with each predicate” means the one reality considered through each quality that applies to it. The note clarifies that the name and attribute refer to realized existence, not merely to an abstract mental idea. — س قده

“Belonging to” here does not mean that the fixed entities are effects produced by existence. It means they are present through existence, like matter through form. They are not independently created things or accidents added to existence. — س قده
This means the names and attributes as concepts.

These “fixed realities”—whether concepts of the divine names and attributes or the possible essences of things—are not independently existing realities. They are distinctions made in thought. They exist only by virtue of an existence that is not their own. If their being intelligible to God depends on their being present to Him, and that presence belongs to them only through something else, then strictly speaking it is their existence that is present and known in itself. We have simply returned to the argument that God knows all things because they exist for Him.
Calling these concepts what is known only replaces what exists and is known in itself with what does so through something else. It explains nothing and may make the argument worse.

Moreover, as has often been pointed out, essences and other general concepts belong to the way souls think. They are abstractions, and some arise from mistakes of imagination. Beings that are entirely free of matter, both in what they are and how they act, do not know by acquiring such concepts. Their knowledge is direct presence. — ط مد ظله
